notes.claim: A higher discharge rate gives a lower capacity reading, and available capacity falls with rising discharge rate approximately as Peukert's law describes.
Lead acid batteries are commonly rated at a 20-hour discharge, and one maker note says a 100 Ah battery rated at C20 may give only 56 Ah in two hours.
An ideal battery has a Peukert exponent of 1.00 and fixed capacity at any current; Victron's default for lead acid is 1.25, and two rated capacities give the exponent.
In Peukert's formula H is the discharge time in hours that the amp-hour rating is based on, so 100 Ah at a 20-hour rate gives H = 20.
Peukert's exponent is a rough approximation: at very high currents the battery gives even less capacity than a fixed exponent predicts.
Cold raises internal resistance and lowers capacity: a battery giving 100 per cent at 27 degrees C typically delivers only about 50 per cent at minus 18 degrees C.

A discharge test ends at an end voltage that depends on how long the discharge lasts: 1.60 V a cell for 5 to 59 minutes, 1.70 V for 1 to 5 hours, 1.75 V for 5 to 8 hours and 1.80 V for 8 to 24 hours. Lesson 3's picture uses 1.75 V a cell, 10.50 V for six cells, for every run, as a simplification.

SOLAS: a ship's emergency accumulator battery must carry the emergency load without recharging, holding its voltage within 12 per cent of nominal through the discharge; for a 24 V battery that is 21.1 V to 26.9 V (computed).

Copper's resistance rises about 0.393 per cent per degree C at 20 degrees C, small beside the doubling of the example battery's internal resistance between 27 and minus 18 degrees C (lesson 3's analogy).
